analysis.one_liner: Lets the FTC fine sellers who gouge prices on essential goods during disasters and pandemics.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced during the COVID-19 pandemic, never received a committee hearing or floor vote and died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it a federal unfair-practice violation, enforced by the Federal Trade Commission, to sell essential goods or services at unconscionably excessive prices during or ahead of a disaster, pandemic, or declared emergency. Prices more than 20 percent above the seller's or the local area's pre-crisis level would be presumed excessive unless higher costs justified them. It would add civil penalties of up to $10,000 per violation, a dedicated phone and online hotline for complaints, and would leave existing state price-gouging laws untouched.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary consumers buying essentials like food, medicine, protective equipment, and fuel during emergencies, who would have a federal recourse when sellers raise prices far above pre-crisis levels.

how_it_helps.text: Makes price gouging on essential goods and services an unfair or deceptive act under the FTC Act during, or in anticipation of, a natural disaster, pandemic, or declared state of emergency [S2][S3].

Sets a 20 percent presumption: a price is presumed unconscionably excessive if it exceeds by 20 percent either the seller's own average price or the local area's average price over the prior 60 days, unless the increase is due to the seller's own higher costs [S3].
Lets the FTC sue violators in federal court for civil penalties of up to $10,000 per violation, in addition to other remedies [S3].
Requires a dedicated FTC hotline and online portal for price-gouging complaints, active during and until 120 days after major disasters or emergencies [S2][S3].
Explicitly preserves existing state price-gouging laws rather than overriding them [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Sellers of essential goods and services — retailers, pharmacies, suppliers of protective equipment, and other vendors — who would face federal penalties and legal exposure for steep emergency-period price increases that are not explained by their own rising costs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Retailers and sellers of essential goods

drawbacks.text: The penalty is capped at $10,000 per violation, which a large seller could treat as a modest cost of doing business during a shortage [S3].

The 'unconscionably excessive' standard turns on comparisons to prior average prices, which can be hard to apply fairly in volatile markets, and the bill's presumption carves out cost-based increases that sellers would be expected to litigate over [S3].
With no cosponsors and no committee action, the bill never underwent any refinement or scrutiny that might have addressed these design questions before the Congress ended [S4][S5].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers, the benefit is straightforward: a federal backstop against sellers charging dramatically more for necessities during the exact moments people can least switch suppliers. The main cost falls on sellers, who retain a cost-based safe harbor, so legitimate supply-chain price increases would not be penalized. The bill's chief weakness is its small penalty cap, which limits deterrence against large national sellers; a well-designed version would likely have scaled penalties to revenue or volume.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, received no cosponsors, and never got a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 116th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Emanuel Cleaver introduced the bill on April 7, 2020, about a month into the COVID-19 national emergency [S1][S5].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, and no further action was ever recorded [S5].
No member of the House joined as a cosponsor at any point [S4].
The bill died at the end of the 116th Congress on January 3, 2021, without a committee or floor vote [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Sellers of essential goods, who retained the ability to raise emergency-period prices well above pre-crisis levels without federal penalty exposure. Consumers gained no new protection, and state price-gouging laws remain the only recourse in most emergencies.

for.name: Rep. Emanuel Cleaver
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to committee; it was never taken up.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and took no recorded action — no hearing, markup, or report — for the remainder of the Congress.

against.name: House leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor; with no committee action, no vote was ever scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: No cosponsors of either party and no recorded votes, so the bill never revealed a partisan pattern of support or opposition.

industries.industry: Retailers and sellers of essential goods (grocers, pharmacies, e-commerce sellers of masks and other pandemic supplies)
industries.note: The bill would expose these sellers to FTC civil penalties for prices more than 20 percent above pre-crisis levels during emergencies, with only cost-based increases exempted. Sellers who raised prices during shortages would see that revenue stream become legally risky; consumers would gain a federal complaint channel.

industries.industry: Hotels, rental car firms, and other travel and lodging providers
industries.note: These industries are frequent targets of state price-gouging rules during hurricanes and other declared emergencies; a federal standard with FTC enforcement would add a second layer of exposure for surge pricing during disasters.
